newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa announces arms disclosure policy.
newsitem.headline: South Africa announces arms disclosure policy.

text.p: South Africa said on Wednesday it would end secrecy surrounding arms deals with other countries, sweeping away the cloak-and-dagger approach of the apartheid era.

Kader Asmal, a member of President Nelson Mandela's cabinet and chairman of the state arms control committee, told a news conference the cabinet had agreed to proposals to provide maximum public disclosure.
"Such a policy is unique internationally in that it seeks to disclose an unprecedented amount of information on arms transfers to the public," Asmal said.
"Nowhere in the world is there total disclosure of all arms transfer details."
Under the new regulations, disclosure to the public would include the total value of a contract, a description of items, the date of export and details of any counter-trade arrangements.
But disclosure of the name of the country buying arms could be witheld at the discretion of the committee, Asmal said.
"Disclosure must be consistent with the need to protect, in some cases, national interests and commercial confidentiality," he said.
South Africa's arms industry expanded quickly during the apartheid years as a major pillar in isolated South Africa's campaign against Soviet-backed liberation movements.

It became resourceful in the face of world sanctions, with the result that it was possibly South Africa's most successful manufacturing sector when Mandela's African National Congress took power in April 1994.
Arms exports soared in 1995 to 1.04 billion rand ($220 million) from 614 million rand in 1992, and 50,000 are employed in about 700 companies in the defence industry.
This year, a proposed $650 million sale of a laser-guided tank firing control system to Syria was reversed after intense international pressure.
